newsitem.title: FRANCE: France grants telecom infrastructure licences.
newsitem.headline: France grants telecom infrastructure licences.

text.p: French telecommunications minister Francois Fillon said he was awarding a licence for a so-called "alternative" telecommunications network to the company France Manche which operates the network in the cross-Channel tunnel.

Speaking to the Anglo-French Chambre of Commerce in London on Thursday evening, Fillon added he would soon also award such licences to MFS Ltd of the U.S., Britain's Colt Telecom Group, which is owned by financial group Fidelity Investments, and French state-owned rail group SNCF.
A text of his speech was sent to Reuters on Friday.

"I have signed today the first licence for an operator of an alternative infrastructure for the company France Manche which operates the tunnel and supplies rental links between Paris and London," Fillon said.
"In the coming days I will deliver the same sort of licences to SNCF, MFS and Colt," he added.
France Manche is one of the two founding companies of the Eurotunnel SA /Plc group, the other being the Chunnel Group in Britain.
Alternative networks are telecommunications networks independent of that run by France Telecom and the licences are part of the liberalisation of the French telecommunications industry.
The Societe Nationale des Chemins de Fer (SNCF) is expected to announce before the end of the year its choice of an industrial operator for its extensive telecoms network.
The candidates are the CEGETEL unit of Generale des Eaux, British Telecom Plc, Mannesmann and SBC, as well as Bouygues Telecom with Italy's STET.
MFS and Colt want to operate networks in Paris, especially catering to business clients.

These alternative networks, as well as mobile telecommunications networks and the future telecoms rivals of France Telecom, will have to use France Telecom's equipment at some stage to connect clients with contacts outside the network.

For this, France Telecom will levy so-called interconnection charges and Fillon is currently conducting a public consultation on this issue until end-November. The new Telecommunications Authority, which will from January 1 be the country's telecoms regulator, is expected to decide on the interconnection charges at the start of 1997.
"I believe that the interconnection charges in France should be comparable to those in force in other countries," Fillon said.

France Telecom is proposing a price range, from 0.16 to 0.26 francs per minute, which is higher than the rates in Britain, where regulator OFTEL earlier this week ordered British Telecom Plc to cut those prices by 12 percent.
Fillon re-iterated that the government planned to sell a first tranche of about 20 percent in France Telecom.
"The state will keep a direct majority stake, (France Telecom's) civil servants will remain civil servants and the state will continue to pay the pensions of the civil servants," he said.

"With this we have been able to pass a law which will turn France Telecom into a limited company on January 1, 1997, and the French government wants to offer from the spring some 20 percent of the capital of France Telecom to investors," he said.
